Beyond Locks and Thread IDs:
Static Data Race Detection Off The Beaten Path

(Extended Version)
Daniel Bund Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Garching, Germany E-mail {daniel.bund,michael.petter}@tum.de    Julian Erhard Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz-Zentrum, Garching, Germany E-mail julian.erhard@cispa.de    Michael Petter Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, Garching, Germany E-mail {daniel.bund,michael.petter}@tum.de    Michael Schwarz Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore E-mail m.schwarz@nus.edu.sg
Abstract

Maintaining an abstraction of the execution history of threads can improve the precision of data race detection in static analysis. Here, we extend the digest framework to handle concurrency constructs and synchronization mechanisms that have been ignored in static race detection. We introduce mechanisms for the commonly used thread barriers, as well as pthread_once, which allows to ensure that an action is executed only once. We also instantiate the framework with an abstraction of locksets held by ancestor threads. We propose a suite of litmus tests to evaluate analyses for these features and compare our implementation to state-of-the-art tools, finding that they lack support.

Keywords: 
data races, concurrency, static program analysis, software verification, abstract interpretation

1 Introduction

Data races are a class of errors that is particularly hard to debug, partially due to the nondeterministic nature of the scheduling, i.e., bugs not materializing in every execution. To ensure correctness of code, particularly in domains where bugs are unacceptable, sound static analyses have been proposed that are guaranteed to flag any potential data race. However, these analyses typically suffer from false positives. For such tools to be practical, the number of false positives must remain manageable [3, 12]. Nevertheless, much of the literature on static data-race detection considers only mutexes and thread creation and joining as synchronization, overlooking less common but equally valid ways to prevent conflicting accesses from occurring concurrently. One such feature are barriers as provided by Pthreads:

Example 1

Figure 1 is a program fragment using barriers. The main thread creates two workers, which compute with the value of a global variable gg and their string argument. The barrier bb is used to ensure that both workers can only perform their computation (line ) after the main thread has set the global in line . Once all three threads have called wait for bb, all of them can proceed. Assuming that the variable gg is only accessed in the three locations given in the program fragment, there is no data race: The write to gg in line  happens before all threads have reached the barrier, and the other two accesses to gg happen later.

On top of synchronization by barriers, we also consider the pthread_once feature library developers often rely on (see the example Figure 4 in Section 3) and two patterns combining reasoning about threads and synchronization by mutexes (see the descendantLocksets example in Figure 8 in Section 5, as well as the creationLocksets examples in Figure 9).

We focus on the temporal aspect of race detection, providing sound methods to prove that two access instructions cannot happen in parallel. This takes different forms: For barriers, our approach determines that certain accesses must happen before others. For pthread_once, this is combined with establishing that all accesses protected by the same pthread_once control variable happen in the same thread and can thus not race, even when their specific order cannot be established. When it comes to reasoning about threads and mutexes, in the descendantLocksets case (Section 5), it is once more must-happen-before relationships that are established, while for creationLocksets (Appendix 0.F), it is only the fact that accesses are in fact ordered by critical sections even though they may not appear to be at first glance. Broadly, these mechanisms fall into two categories: barriers, pthread_once, and descendant locksets use additional history information to establish must-happen-before relationships between accesses, whereas creation locksets (Appendix 0.F) extend conventional lockset reasoning by recognizing protection through critical sections spanning multiple threads.

Our approach is parametric in the other important ingredient of static race detection, namely a may-alias analysis, and can be combined with different such analyses to obtain different speed–precision tradeoffs.

We base our work on digest-driven abstract interpretation. Abstract interpretation [4] is a principled way to overapproximate the concrete semantics of programs using abstract domains. Digests [27] were originally designed as a mechanism to improve the precision of thread-modular value analyses using abstract interpretation. Digests allow an analysis to distinguish program points as well as the states of shared variables according to the execution history observed by the thread executing the statement. They thus generalize trace partitioning [20] to concurrent programs, providing concurrency-sensitivity that can be configured independently of the analysis domain. In the result computed by an analysis with digests, potentially reachable accesses to shared variables are annotated with digests, i.e., an abstraction of the execution history observed by the thread in question. This can be exploited to enhance the precision of sound static data race detection [25]: When considering two accesses to a shared variable, both annotated with a digest, data races can be excluded when the two accesses cannot happen concurrently—as judged by their digests.

While previous work [27, 24, 25] proposes digests for history information such as whether the execution is single-threaded or multi-threaded, or which mutexes are locked by the current thread, libraries such as Pthreads offer further concurrency and synchronization primitives, which have often been ignored. In particular, we provide digests for barriers, a mechanism to synchronize multiple threads. To do so, we extend the semantic framework underlying the digest framework to actions that involve more than two threads (Section 2). We show how digests are used to argue about whether two arbitrary operations may possibly happen in parallel11 1 While may happen concurrently is perhaps the more accurate term, we use may happen in parallel for consistency with the literature on MHP analysis., which is not only a key ingredient of our barrier digest but also paves the way towards further applications of the digest framework.

We show in Section 4 how a history abstraction, i.e., a digest, relating to the operations performed on the barrier, is used to deduce race freedom for the programs using barriers, such as Example 1. There, the predicate ||?||^{?}, introduced for checking whether two accesses to the same variable may race, is used for a different purpose in the definition of the barrier digest itself, to determine whether a sufficient number of threads may wait at the barrier at the same time.

Section 3 proposes a digest for pthread_once for more precise data-race detection. pthread_once is a feature used in particular by library developers to ensure that some code is executed exactly once.

Sometimes a thread locks a mutex before creating child threads and does not release it until certain protected operations have completed. This pattern requires intricate handling beyond existing per-thread lockset analyses. Partially inspired by Lu et al. [19], we propose a way of handling such patterns with digests in Section 5. Another pattern, where locks are held by a thread during the entire execution of its child is covered in Section 6. We implemented the proposed digests in an abstract interpreter. The experiments we conducted on a set of hand-crafted examples using these constructs are discussed in Section 7.

2 Digest-Driven Data Race Detection

At a high level, digest-driven data race detection [25] proceeds in two phases. First, an abstract interpreter propagates abstract program states indexed by digests, compact summaries of the execution history observed by the current thread, such as its thread id, currently held locks, or completed synchronization events. Several digests, each tailored to a different aspect of concurrency, can be active simultaneously and jointly index the abstract states. Whenever the analysis reaches a shared-memory access, it records the access together with its digest. Second, the race detector considers pairs of accesses that may refer to the same memory location and of which at least one is a write. It applies a may-happen-in-parallel predicate to each active digest: if any one of them establishes from the aspect of the histories it records that the accesses cannot occur concurrently, the pair is discarded; otherwise, it is reported as a potential data race. Thus, digests provide the concurrency information used both to partition abstract states during the analysis and to rule out infeasible races afterward.

We next introduce the local trace semantics underlying the digest framework, and formally define digests and the may-happen-in-parallel predicate. The local trace semantics precisely describes concurrent programs while abstracting away irrelevant details such as the order of local actions of independent threads, which are differentiated in an interleaving semantics. It has served as the justification for thread-modular analyses and the digest framework. Observable and observing actions play a key role: they may be ordered relative to actions of other threads. Previous work fixed observing actions to arity two, so features such as pthread_once or barriers could not be expressed. We directly present our generalization to observing actions of arbitrary arity. Previous work encoded atomic global accesses using cumbersome atomicity mutexes. We instead allow operations to be both observable and observing, avoiding atomicity mutexes.

2.1 Local Trace Semantics

A program is a set of labelled control-flow graphs (CFGs), one for each thread entry point. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the CFG nodes (program points), 𝒜​c​t\mathcal{A}ct the actions, and ℰ⊆𝒩×𝒜​c​t×𝒩\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{N}\times\mathcal{A}ct\times\mathcal{N} the labelled CFG edges. Program text can be translated into this representation using standard compiler techniques.

A local trace encodes the history of one ego thread — the thread whose perspective is taken — and the parts of other threads’ histories it can know. The knowledge comes from observing actions, which observe observable actions of other threads. Examples include locking (observing), unlocking (observable), and global-variable accesses (both). Table 1 summarizes observing and observable actions. Further, there are local actions (neither observing nor observable).

A local trace contains one action-interleaved configuration sequence per appearing thread. Each sequence follows a path through the CFG and is locally consistent: its local-variable reads, writes, and taken guards agree [28]. This sequence is the thread’s swim-lane, ordered by the program order →p​o\to_{po}. For each non-main thread, a →c\to_{c} edge connects its create action to the first node of its swim-lane. Observing and observable actions induce further dependencies between configurations, possibly across threads, ensuring global consistency. For example—given mutex mm from the set of mutexes 𝒮\mathcal{S}—there is a dependency →m\to_{m} from an unlock(m) to the next lock(m) operation, where each unlock of mm (and the initialization action) has at most one outgoing edge →m\to_{m} and each lock has exactly one incoming edge →m\to_{m} (for the first lock, this edge originates at the endpoint of a special observable action initMT22 2 This program-start action executes first and is observed when a mutex is first locked or a global first accessed. We elide this purely technical action henceforth. ). Thus, mutex operations are totally ordered, so at most one thread holds a mutex at a time. Likewise, a →g\to_{g} edge connects each access to global gg to the next, encoding atomic global accesses. We revisit its relation to race reporting at the section’s end. In a local trace, then,

  • •

    Each swim-lane is locally consistent;

  • •

    Each auxiliary order (e.g., creation order →c\to_{c} and mutex orders →m\to_{m}) meets its requirements;

  • •

    The transitive closure of the combined program and auxiliary orders is acyclic, with a least element representing the main thread’s initial configuration and a maximal element.

The maximal element is the ego thread’s last configuration, ensuring that the local trace represents one thread’s perspective. Figure 2 shows an example representation for a local trace of the program in Figure 1 with ego thread w​1w1.

Let 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} denote the program’s local traces, defined inductively later. For now, let init⊂𝒯\textsf{init}\subset{\mathcal{T}} contain the initial local traces, each consisting only of the main thread’s initial configuration. Data Races.

Since local trace semantics totally orders all accesses to a global gg via →g\to_{g} edges, its use for data-race detection may seem surprising. Schwarz and Erhard [25] show that it is possible: bidirectional trace compatibility coincides with the intuitive notion of two accesses to a global being unordered.

Definition 1

Traces t0t_{0} and t1t_{1} ending in nodes u0u_{0} and u1u_{1} with outgoing edges (u0,act0,u0′)(u_{0},\textsf{act}_{0},u_{0}^{\prime}) and (u1,act1,u1′)(u_{1},\textsf{act}_{1},u_{1}^{\prime}) where act0\textsf{act}_{0} and act1\textsf{act}_{1} are accesses to the same global variable, are bidirectionally trace compatible, if, with appropriately lifted ⟦e⟧\llbracket e\rrbracket,

∃t′∈𝒯:None≠⟦(u0,act0,u0′)⟧​(t0,⟦(u1,act1,u1′)⟧​(t1,t′))∧None≠⟦(u1,act1,u1′)⟧​(t1,⟦(u0,act0,u0′)⟧​(t0,t′)).\begin{array}[]{lll}\exists t^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{T}}&:&\textbf{None}\neq\llbracket(u_{0},\textsf{act}_{0},u_{0}^{\prime})\rrbracket(t_{0},\llbracket(u_{1},\textsf{act}_{1},u_{1}^{\prime})\rrbracket(t_{1},t^{\prime}))\land\\ &&\textbf{None}\neq\llbracket(u_{1},\textsf{act}_{1},u_{1}^{\prime})\rrbracket(t_{1},\llbracket(u_{0},\textsf{act}_{0},u_{0}^{\prime})\rrbracket(t_{0},t^{\prime})).\end{array}

This means that the accesses can immediately follow each other in either order, matching the intuitive notion of being unordered.

Proposition 1

Two accesses to a global variable gg are racy in the intuitive sense if and only if at least one is a write and traces t0t_{0} and t1t_{1} ending in the respective CFG predecessors exist, s.t. they are bidirectionally trace compatible.

Proof

Similar to [25, Theorem 1]; see Appendix 0.B.∎

2.2 Digests and Digest-Driven Data Race Detection

Digests [28, 24, 27] abstract thread histories and can refine abstract interpretations of concurrent programs. They exploit that some thread histories are incompatible, a notion transferable from local traces to digests.

We require digests to be computable inductively. For the initial set of digests at the program start, we define

init𝒜♯={α𝒜​t∣t∈init}.\textsf{init}^{\sharp}_{\mathcal{A}}=\{\alpha_{\mathcal{A}}\,t\mid t\in\textsf{init}\}. (2)

Digest-Driven Abstract Interpretation.

An analysis can be refined using any admissible digest. We quickly present the requirements for an analysis. An analysis constraint system is obtained from the concrete constraint system by replacing sets of traces with an analysis domain and concrete transfer functions with abstract ones. Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the abstract domain used by the analysis, which forms a complete lattice with operations join ⊔\sqcup and meet ⊓\sqcap. A monotonic function γ𝒟:𝒟→2𝒯\gamma_{\mathcal{D}}:\mathcal{D}\to 2^{{\mathcal{T}}} provides the concretization of a given domain element. The analysis must define abstract transfer functions ⟦⋅⟧♯\left\llbracket\cdot\right\rrbracket^{\sharp}, as well as abstract versions new♯\textsf{new}^{\sharp} and init♯\textsf{init}^{\sharp} of new and init. Given soundness of ⟦⋅⟧♯\left\llbracket\cdot\right\rrbracket^{\sharp}, new♯\textsf{new}^{\sharp}, and init♯\textsf{init}^{\sharp} w.r.t. their concrete counterparts, related by γ𝒟\gamma_{\mathcal{D}}, and the monotonicity of ⟦⋅⟧♯\left\llbracket\cdot\right\rrbracket^{\sharp} and ⟦⋅⟧\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket, it follows that the concretization of a solution of the analysis constraint system is greater than the least solution of the concrete constraint system (see [24, Theorem 1]).

When refining an analysis with a digest, the constraint system is adapted by splitting unknowns according to digests, yielding a constraint system of form:

Proposition 2

Refining a sound abstract interpretation of a concurrent program with an admissible digest yields a sound abstract interpretation.

Proof

By giving a digest-refined concrete semantics and showing that soundness of the original abstract interpretation w.r.t. the original semantics carries over to the refined setting. See Appendix 0.B for details.∎

As examples, we consider the lockset digest, which tracks each thread’s currently held locks (see Figure 3), and the thread id digest for dynamically created threads:

Schwarz et al. [27] propose a digest computing thread ids for pthreads. It identifies threads by the sequence of create edges involved in their creation: the main thread receives main, a thread it creates along edge ee receives main⋅e\textsf{main}\cdot e, and so on. To account for cycles in the creation history caused by recursively creating threads or threads being created in a loop, non-definite thread ids are used. For details, see [27]. In the rest of the paper, we use generic thread ids with the following assumptions. A thread id is information that remains constant for all operations of a given concrete thread and can be projected from a digest 𝒜1{\mathcal{A}_{1}} by πtid:𝒜1→TID\pi_{\textsf{tid}}:{\mathcal{A}_{1}}\to\textsf{TID}. We further assume the existence of functions:

  • •

    unique:TID→Bool\textsf{unique}:\textsf{TID}\to\textsf{Bool} checking whether, in any execution, at most one concrete thread can have this abstract thread id.

  • •

    must_anc:TID→2TID\textsf{must\_anc}:\textsf{TID}\to 2^{\textsf{TID}} returning the set of must ancestors, i.e., threads that must have been involved in the creation of the current thread.

  • •

    may_create:𝒜1→2TID\textsf{may\_create}:{\mathcal{A}_{1}}\to 2^{\textsf{TID}} returning the may-created thread ids, i.e., child-thread ids the ego thread may have created given a digest.

The product of admissible digests is also an admissible digest [24]. This allows for a modular design where digests tracking different aspects of the history can seamlessly be combined during an analysis.

May-Happen-In-Parallel Predicate.

Digests support reasoning about the temporal separation aspect of data races [25]. For two accesses to race, they must potentially happen concurrently: by Proposition 1, there must be bidirectionally trace-compatible traces ending just before them. Thus, compatibility of digests, an abstraction of local-trace compatibility, can exclude data races. Two digests A0A_{0} and A1A_{1} are compatible with an edge ee and each other if there are traces t0t_{0} and t1t_{1} with these digests that are compatible with ee and each other. Thus, if two digests are not bidirectionally compatible, the corresponding traces are not either. This yields a first definition of a may-happen-in-parallel predicate

||e1,e2?:𝒜→𝒜→{false,⊤}||_{e_{1},e_{2}}^{?}:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{A}}\to\{\textsf{false},\top\}

for checking whether two accesses to a variable may race, where e1e_{1} and e2e_{2} are the CFG edges in question. We outline the detailed requirements for ||e1,e2?||_{e_{1},e_{2}}^{?} in Appendix 0.A. When edges are clear or irrelevant, we write ||?||^{?}. The answers form the lattice false⊑⊤\textsf{false}\sqsubseteq\top. For product digests, answers can be combined using meet (⊓\sqcap). For thread ids, the ||?||^{?} definition arising from bidirectional digest compatibility is maximally precise. However, this is not the case for all digests. For instance, with the lockset digest, two actions with overlapping locksets cannot run concurrently, so the corresponding concrete accesses cannot race. However, bidirectional digest compatibility cannot infer this, because overlapping locksets need not prevent the respective accesses to a global gg from directly following each other in the →g\to_{g} order. Thus, one may instead provide a more precise ||?||^{?} and justify it directly w.r.t. bidirectional trace compatibility. We generalize ||?e1,e2||^{?}_{e_{1},e_{2}} to show that two arbitrary-action edges e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} cannot happen in parallel: introduce a fresh global variable and replace the actions by writes to it, yielding edges e1′,e2′e_{1}^{\prime},e_{2}^{\prime}. Then A1||?e1,e2A2A_{1}||^{?}_{e_{1},e_{2}}A_{2} is defined as A1||?e1′,e2′A2A_{1}||^{?}_{e_{1}^{\prime},e_{2}^{\prime}}A_{2}.

Race Detection.

Schwarz and Erhard [25] give a data race detection algorithm using digests. First, one performs digest-driven abstract interpretation, collecting digests associated with accesses. Then, for each shared memory location, one iterates over all access pairs. For accesses at edges e1e_{1} and e2e_{2} with digests A1A_{1} and A2A_{2}, a potential race is flagged if at least one access is a write and A1||?e1,e2A2=⊤A_{1}||^{?}_{e_{1},e_{2}}A_{2}=\top.

3 Synchronization via pthread_once

Pthreads offers a mechanism for executing code at most once. This enables resource initialization before thread access, such as opening a shared log file or database connection. Application developers can place such code in main, but library developers do not control main and instead rely on pthread_once [2]. It provides a type for control variables (which we assume are from set 𝒪\mathcal{O}) and a function pthread_once(o,f) which executes ff and sets oo if it is unset, and otherwise does nothing. The system makes running ff and setting oo appear atomic. Consider the program in Figure 4. init_lib must allocate and initialize the device before any other library function runs. pthread_once ensures that init_lib is called exactly once and that the device is initialized before use.

pthread_once is often overlooked by static analyzers or abstracted very crudely. With digests, it can be handled precisely without complicating the underlying analysis; all handling happens inside the digest. This excludes two race classes: within the called function and between initialization and later code.

Extension of the concrete semantics.

We introduce a new observable action initO​(o)\textsf{initO}(o) to initialize a control variable oo at program start55 5 Unlike library developers, a whole-program analyzer can conceptually insert helper code at program start, so this action does not negate the need for pthread_once. and compile pthread_ once(o,f) to a sequence calling startO​(o)\textsf{startO}(o), branching on ran​(o)\textsf{ran}(o), executing the inlined code from ff if ran​(o)\textsf{ran}(o) is false, and finally performing endO​(o)\textsf{endO}(o). Here, initO​(o)\textsf{initO}(o) and endO​(o)\textsf{endO}(o) are observable, while startO​(o)\textsf{startO}(o) is observing, analogous to initMT/unlock​(a)\textsf{initMT}/\textsf{unlock}(a) and lock​(a)\textsf{lock}(a) for mutex aa. The once order →o\to_{o} follows

the mutex-order requirements from Section 2.1. The actions Pos​(ran​(o))\textsf{Pos}(\textsf{ran}(o)) and Neg​(ran​(o))\textsf{Neg}(\textsf{ran}(o)) guard whether the code associated with pthread_once is to be executed: the former returns a local trace only when endO​(o)\textsf{endO}(o) appears in the trace, and the latter only when it does not.66 6 Recursively calling pthread_once(o,f) is not conclusively specified in the standard; here, we decided to go for the behavior of glibc, which deadlocks upon such calls. The program in Figure 5 corresponds to the one in Figure 4 after abstracting away details and expressing pthread_once as above.

A digest for this feature (Figure 6) may then track two sets in a tuple (A,C)(A,C):

  • •

    A set AA of active control variables, i.e., those for which the ego thread is currently inside the section between startO​(o)\textsf{startO}(o) and endO​(o)\textsf{endO}(o).

  • •

    A set CC of completed control variables, i.e., those for which the associated fragment has surely been run, as a call to endO​(o)\textsf{endO}(o) was observed.

The guards Pos​(ran​(o))\textsf{Pos}(\textsf{ran}(o)) and Neg​(ran​(o))\textsf{Neg}(\textsf{ran}(o)) check whether oo has already completed, i.e., whether it is in CC. startO​(o)\textsf{startO}(o) adds oo to the active set, and endO​(o)\textsf{endO}(o) moves it from the active to the completed set.

||?||^{?} can then be defined as:

(A,C)||?(A′,C′)={false if ​(A∩(A′∪C′)≠∅)∨(A′∩(A∪C)≠∅)⊤otherwise,(A,C)\;||^{?}\;(A^{\prime},C^{\prime})=\begin{cases}\textsf{false}&\text{ if }(A\cap(A^{\prime}\cup C^{\prime})\neq\emptyset)\lor(A^{\prime}\cap(A\cup C)\neq\emptyset)\\ \top&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

i.e., accesses may not race when a control variable is active during both accesses, or active in one and completed in the other.

Example 2

Consider again the program in Figure 5. An analysis using the digest from Figure 6 succeeds in establishing race freedom. \hfill\squareforqed

Proposition 3

The digest given above is admissible, and its predicate ||?||^{?} sound.

See Appendix 0.C for the proof (by contradiction) and an extended digest making the analysis of global variables more precise.

4 Synchronization via Barriers

Pthreads provides barriers: after initialization by calling pthread_barrier_init​(b,c)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_init}(b,c) for a barrier bb and capacity c∈ℕ+c\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, callers to pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b) block until cc threads have called it, at which point all waiters are unblocked. Figure 1 shows a barrier example whose pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b) calls may all happen in parallel.

In fact, this always needs to be the case, as any call to pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b) happening after another call has returned, cannot contribute to reaching the required capacity. The predicate ||?||^{?} also detects stuck executions when fewer than c−1c-1 other pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b) calls may happen in parallel. Passing a barrier reveals cross-thread information that excludes some races.

Extension of the concrete semantics.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a set of barriers. For presentation, we initially assume static capacities (eliminating pthread_barrier_init) and replace each pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b) with barrier_N_record​(b);\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b); barrier_N_check​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_check}(b), where N∈ℕ+N\in\mathbb{N}^{+} is bb’s capacity. The action barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b) is non-blocking and observable, i.e., the local trace ending in it is recorded at the corresponding unknown. The action barrier_N_check​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_check}(b) is observing and NN-ary, incorporating local traces stored at the unknown corresponding to barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b), i.e., those ending in that action.77 7 This uses our generalization to higher-arity observing actions. Figure 2 shows an example local trace.

By construction of the constraint system, for ⟦e⟧​(t0,…,tN−1)\llbracket e\rrbracket(t_{0},\dots,t_{N-1}) for an edge e=(u,barrier_N_check​(b),v)e=(u,\textsf{barrier\_N\_check}(b),v), t0t_{0} is a local trace ending in uu with last action barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b), and the other N−1N-1 local traces provided as an argument also end in barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b), as that is the action observed by the check action. The call yields Some ​t′\textbf{Some }t^{\prime} only if its arguments are distinct and their union, augmented with dependency edges from the record endpoints to the check endpoint, is a local trace. For each barrier bb, the barrier order →b\to_{b} goes from nodes with an incoming edge barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b) to those with an incoming edge barrier_N_check​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_check}(b); call these sets B+B^{+} and B−B^{-}, respectively. Each B+B^{+} node has at most 11 outgoing →b\to_{b} edge, while B−B^{-} node has exactly NN incoming →b\to_{b} edges, including one from the control-flow predecessor, i.e., the thread passing the barrier was involved in the barrier being passed. This order then forms part of the causality order of a local trace. Consider the NN subtraces ending at B+B^{+} nodes that directly →b\to_{b}-precede a B−B^{-} node. None of these subtraces may contain any of the relevant calls to barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b). This ensures that all NN calls happened in parallel.

Before deriving a digest tracking information about barriers, we first observe that for any digest that provides the predicate ||?||^{?} for checking for data races and does not track information about barriers, i.e., is unaffected by executing actions barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b) and barrier_N_check​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_check}(b), a definition of ⟦_,barrier_N_check(b)⟧𝒜♯\left\llbracket\_,\textsf{barrier\_N\_check(b)}\right\rrbracket^{\sharp}_{{\mathcal{A}}} can be given that detects some instances where the execution must become stuck: ⟦_,barrier_N_check(b)⟧𝒜♯(A0,…,AN−1)=\left\llbracket\_,\textsf{barrier\_N\_check(b)}\right\rrbracket^{\sharp}_{{\mathcal{A}}}(A_{0},\dots,A_{N-1})=

{Some ​A0if ∀i,j∈[0,N−1]:i≠j⟹Ai||?Aj=⊤Noneotherwise\begin{array}[]{l}\begin{cases}\textbf{Some }A_{0}&\text{if }\forall i,j\in[0,N-1]:i\neq j\implies A_{i}||^{?}A_{j}=\top\\ \textbf{None}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\end{array}

This uses the predicate ||?||^{?} to check whether the NN calls to barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b) can all happen in parallel. When this is not the case, the execution must become stuck, and None is returned, denoting unreachability. The predicate thus turns out to be not only useful when considering whether accesses can happen in parallel, but also when considering richer synchronization primitives.

Example 3

Consider Figure 1 and assume that the developer has, by mistake, surrounded calls to pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b) with locking and unlocking of mutex mm. Then, one thread reaches the call to pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b) while holding mm. However, it will not release mm until the barrier is passed, and the other threads do not call pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b) until they have acquired mm. The execution deadlocks. With the lockset digest from [25] with the definition of ||?||^{?} returning false when locksets overlap, the analysis will detect this as {m}||?{m}=false\{m\}||^{?}\{m\}=\textsf{false}. \hfill\squareforqed

Showing certain accesses unreachable may improve the precision of race detection. If a digest tracks thread ids, we can define a more precise digest that excludes more races by tracking barriers passed by the current thread and observed barrier actions of other threads. If, for two accesses, one thread knows that the other has passed a barrier that it has not yet passed, the accesses are ordered w.r.t. each other and thus not bidirectionally compatible and not racy.

The new digest is the product of the original digest 𝒜1{\mathcal{A}_{1}} and two components88 8 The tracking of separate components for RR and OO is to simplify presentation here: Whenever the thread id in AA is unique, RR can be reconstructed from OO.:

  • •

    a set R⊆ℬR\subseteq\mathcal{B} of barriers for which the current thread has called barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b)

  • •

    a map O:TID→2ℬO:\textsf{TID}\to 2^{\mathcal{B}} from thread ids to sets of barriers for which the respective thread has been observed to have called barrier_N_record​(b)\textsf{barrier\_N\_record}(b).

The corresponding right-hand sides for the digest are given in Figure 7 in terms of those for 𝒜1{\mathcal{A}_{1}}. The predicate then is given by: (A0,R0,O0)||?(A1,R1,O1)=(A_{0},R_{0},O_{0})\;||^{?}\;(A_{1},R_{1},O_{1})=

=(A0||?𝒜1A1)⊓{falseif ​(unique​(πtid​A0)∧O1​(πtid​A0)⊈R0)∨(unique​(πtid​A1)∧O0​(πtid​A1)⊈R1)⊤otherwise\begin{array}[]{l}\qquad=(A_{0}\;||^{?}_{{\mathcal{A}_{1}}}\;A_{1})\sqcap\begin{cases}\textsf{false}&\text{if }(\textsf{unique}\,(\pi_{\textsf{tid}}\,A_{0})\land O_{1}\,(\pi_{\textsf{tid}}\,A_{0})\not\subseteq R_{0})\\ &\quad\lor(\textsf{unique}\,(\pi_{\textsf{tid}}\,A_{1})\land O_{0}\,(\pi_{\textsf{tid}}\,A_{1})\not\subseteq R_{1})\\ \top&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\end{array}

On top of the predicate for the base digests, this exploits the fact that if A0A_{0} is unique, any of its actions that have been observed by the other thread must already have happened for the accesses to potentially happen concurrently.

Example 4

Consider again Figure 1 and assume a digest identifies all threads as unique99 9 This is, e.g., the case for the digest-based thread ids abstracting creation history [27]. and assigns them ids main, w1, and w2. The access in main happens before calling pthread_barrier_wait​(b)\textsf{pthread\_barrier\_wait}(b), and has digest (A0,∅,{})(A_{0},\emptyset,\{\}); the worker accesses have digests (Aj,{b},{main↦{b},w1↦{b},w2↦{b}})(A_{j},\{b\},\{\textsf{main}\mapsto\{b\},\textsf{w1}\mapsto\{b\},\textsf{w2}\mapsto\{b\}\}) for some AjA_{j}, where we omit empty bindings. As πtid​A0=main\pi_{\textsf{tid}}\,A_{0}=\textsf{main}, unique main holds but {b}⊈∅\{b\}\not\subseteq\emptyset, the write in main happens before any of the reads, and race-freedom is shown. \hfill\squareforqed

Proposition 4

The digest given above is admissible, and its predicate ||?||^{?} sound.

The proof is by contradiction; see Appendix 0.D. This digest generalizes straightforwardly to tracking how often barriers have been waited for, possibly stopping exact bookkeeping at a fixed constant kk to avoid a blowup. Conversely, for a more tractable analysis, one can switch to an abstract digest to avoid keeping track of exact sets, along the lines of [24].

Remark 1

Our implementation supports dynamic barrier capacities and pointer-based accesses. Barriers may also be used for inter-process communication, but since the Goblint framework does not support process-level concurrency, our implementation soundly and coarsely treats such barriers as no-ops.

5 Synchronization via Mutexes and Creation Orders

While previous sections covered features that are often completely unhandled, here we deal with complex patterns combining thread creation and mutexes: Creating threads while holding a mutex can simulate barriers on platforms lacking them. Also, then, worker threads do not have to wait for one another:

Example 5

In Figure 8, main creates workers i1i_{1} and i2i_{2} while holding mm. Each worker initializes, then immediately acquires and releases mm. These locks occur only after main unlocks mm, so worker accesses to g follow main’s access and cannot race. Notably, i1i_{1} need not wait for i2i_{2} to reach the lock.

For accesses in thread i0i_{0} and a thread i1i_{1} it created, the following conditions rule out conflicts via mutex mm. At the first access, we require that

  1. 1.

    i1i_{1} was created in i0i_{0}, ensuring i0i_{0} is its ancestor. This check matters because an ancestor of i0i_{0} might otherwise have created i1i_{1}, enabling races.

  2. 2.

    At all of those creations, mm is locked—c.f. lockset digest (Figure 3).

  3. 3.

    mm was not unlocked after any such creation.

Note that i1i_{1} does not need to be a child of i0i_{0}, but can be more generally a descendant. So, we account for transitive creations of i1i_{1}, enhancing the precision.

At the second access, we record which threads have locked each mutex. We can exclude a race if a lock of mm has happened at some point after the creation in i0i_{0} in the created thread or—for the same reason as above—one of its descendants. If mm was locked in iHi_{H}, this is the case if i0i_{0} must be an ancestor of iHi_{H}. We describe a suitable digest in Appendix 0.E.

6 Digests for Creation Locksets

The pattern described in Section 5 is not the only one where thread creations with mutexes held can ensure mutual exclusion. This time, we are interested in programs where a mutex mm is held in i0i_{0} throughout the entire execution of a descendant thread i1i_{1}. In consequence, i1i_{1} is protected in some way by mm. This may sometimes be useful: Imagine, e.g., that a thread needs to do two expensive computations in parallel while having exclusive access to a global. Then, it may spawn a new thread while holding the protecting mutex to do one part of the work, while performing some other work in another task. Before releasing the mutex again, the worker thread is joined again. While this is probably more common for programming languages such as Go, where thread creation is cheap, it applies just as well to C programs, as we show in the next example:

Example 6

Consider the program given in Figure 9. Throughout the entire execution of w​o​r​kwork, the mutex mm is locked. As mm is also in the lockset at the access to g in t​1t1, this access cannot race with the one in w​o​r​kwork.

Note that it is important to record that a mutex mm is locked in the creator thread i0i_{0} and held throughout the execution of a descendant thread i1i_{1}, as it does not protect i1i_{1} from accesses happening in i0i_{0}. To detect that i1i_{1} is protected from i0i_{0} with mm, we propose the following conditions:

  1. 1.

    i1i_{1} was transitively created in i0i_{0}, ensuring i0i_{0} must be an ancestor of it. We require the latter condition for the same reason as given in Section 5—there should be no alternative way of creating i0i_{0} other than via i1i_{1}.

  2. 2.

    At all of those creations, mm must be locked, as recorded by the lockset digest.

  3. 3.

    There exists no unlock of mm while i1i_{1} may run in parallel.

For the last point, one can compute the ids of the descendant threads running in parallel by determining all threads that were transitively created from the current thread and subtracting threads that were joined back. Using the thread id digest, we obtain the former. For the latter information, we use the join digest suggested by Schwarz and Erhard [24]. Appendix 0.F gives a digest for checking the conditions above.

7 Experiments and Benchmark Set

We enhanced the Goblint [23] static analyzer to support pthread_once, barriers, and complex interactions between thread creation and mutex locking. The implementations deviate slightly from the presentation here: they support Pthreads directly rather than idealized primitives and use abstract digests in the sense of [24]. For thread-creation and mutex-locking interactions, they use mixed flow-sensitivity [29] to compute abstract digests at global unknowns.

We evaluate scalability and runtime on 60k–80k-LOC GNU Coreutils. Their size precludes ground-truth annotations, but they allow measuring the runtime impact of the new digests against a minimal baseline and the SV-Comp configuration. We ran each benchmark on Ubuntu 26.04 with a 2.5 GHz Intel Core i7-11700, a 5-minute timeout, and a 20 GB memory limit. Table 2 shows the cost of the enhanced synchronization features. It is most pronounced for the locked-creation feature. For df, locked creation handling adds 30.5%30.5\% to the baseline time. However, across ≈\approx 30,000 SV-Comp benchmarks enabling the enhanced synchronization features increased total runtime by ≈2%\approx 2\%, which is negligible.

We also compare our implementation with other static analyzers. We gathered 90 small benchmarks, 20–70 lines of code each, testing the correct handling of each of our four features: 28 pthread_once, 26 barriers, 18 creationLockset, and 18 descendantLockset tests. Each file contains one focused test annotated with the expected ground truth and sometimes motivated by a real-world use case. Our main goal is to determine whether analyzers can correctly certify the absence of data races in the presence of these features. A false positive is an unexpected warning; avoiding them is crucial for the acceptance of static analyzers in practice. Conversely, a false negative is a missed race; even one compromises soundness. We encode the desired behavior as SV-Comp verdicts. We compared our implementation with CPAChecker [1], Dartagnan [7], UGemcutter [14], ESBMC-kind [8], and RacerF [5]. We also wanted to check whether soundness concerns about [19] carry over to the implementation, but the code is unavailable and the authors did not respond to inquiries.

Table 3 summarizes the experiment, detailed in Appendix 0.G. The benchmark set reveals no false positives or false negatives in our implementation. Since our implementation builds on abstract interpretation, it may produce false positives on other programs with the considered features.

All tools treat barriers in a sound way (which can be trivially achieved by not providing specific handling), they however do not exploit the information completely to reduce false positives. Dartagnan and UGemcutter avoid false negatives but return ERROR and UNKNOWN, respectively, when barriers or pthread_once are present. For pthread_once, CPAChecker, RacerF, and ESBMC-kind miss races, but do not produce false positives except for RacerF. All tools miss races in the creationLockset and descendantLockset categories, demonstrating unsound behavior. Dartagnan, ESBMC-kind, and UGemcutter produce no false positives. We hope contributing these tests to Sv-Comp will encourage tools to support these features and spur competition.

8 Related Work

Local traces and digests were proposed in a series of papers on thread-modular value analyses [27, 28, 24, 26]. Recent work [25] re-uses them for race detection. We generalize both to cover more synchronization mechanisms, and show that ||?||^{?} can check whether two actions may run concurrently, which we use for barriers.

Terauchi [37] presents an approach for framing race-freedom of programs as a typing problem, which in turn is solved using rational linear programming. It covers classical lock-based synchronization and mechanisms rarely supported by static analyses, including signaling, semaphores, and read-write locks. However, the approach differs from ours both in the used techniques, type-checking rather than abstract interpretation, and in the considered synchronization mechanisms.

Barriers.

Barriers have been widely studied [16, 21, 15, 22], including analyses of OpenMP-style barriers [18, 36, 35]. In OpenMP, all threads in a team share the same code and must arrive at the syntactically same barrier, so code before a barrier cannot run in parallel with code after it. This does not carry over to Pthreads: different syntactic calls to wait may belong together, and the capacity of a barrier need not equal the number of running threads. Here, we focus on work on Pthreads-style barriers. Mittermayr and Blieberger [21] extend the use of Kronecker algebra from the static analysis of semaphores to barriers. Kokologiannakis and Vafeiadis [15] speed up stateless model checking by merging interleavings that differ only in barrier-arrival order. There, it is required that the initial capacity of a barrier is an upper bound to the number of wait calls that happen in parallel. The analysis is justified w.r.t. a execution graph semantics. Murthy et al. [22] verify (using SPIN) a distributed phaser, a synchronization construct similar to barriers, but do not analyze code using it. Le et al. [16] propose a separation-logic using bounded partial permissions to show that participating threads execute in lockstep phases separated by barriers, thereby excluding races across phases. Their approach and others [10] rely on user annotations; ours is fully automatic. Jeremiassen and Eggers [11] split executions into barrier-delimited phases to determine which sections cannot run concurrently, aiming to reduce compiler-introduced false sharing and cache misses, while Das et al. [6] do so to reduce the instrumentation overhead of dynamic approaches.

Feature pthread_once.

For pthread_once, missing support has been noted as a limitation [30, 17]; to our knowledge, ours is the first analysis beyond syntactic checks [32], both for race detection or static analysis more broadly.

Mutexes and Creation Orders.

In static analysis, research on the patterns from Section 5 is sparse. To our knowledge, only Lu et al. [19] explicitly use it to exclude races, via Segmented Thread-Sensitive Control Flow Graphs. This analysis is not justified w.r.t. a concrete semantics and is unsound on several litmus tests. They also describe mutexes held throughout descendant-thread execution, but give no analysis to detect this pattern; to our knowledge, ours is the first. Dynamic race-prediction techniques [31, 13, 9, 33] reason about ordering constraints induced by locks and other dependencies to determine which re-orderings of an observed execution are possible. This resembles our use of digests as synchronization histories to rule out parallel accesses, but the analysis problem differs substantially. Predictive analyses start from a single execution and seek to weaken its observed ordering without admitting infeasible re-orderings; our sound static analysis overapproximates all executions and must warn unless it can establish that the relevant accesses are ordered in every execution, not just those arising from re-orderings. The descendant-lockset construction establishes the same must-happen-before relationship that CP/WCP-style rules derive from lock synchronization — if a thread is known to acquire a specific mutex before another thread (in our case because the first thread is statically known to be an ancestor of the second and to hold the mutex when the descendant is created), then the release by the first thread must precede the acquire by the second thread. Unlike predictive analyses, which reason over a single trace, our analysis establishes this ordering soundly across all executions. Sulzmann and Thiemann [34] extend dynamic lockset reasoning with cross-thread critical sections, in which an event may be protected by an acquire–release pair executed by another thread when it must occur between them. This captures the same pattern as our creationLocksets: a mutex held by an ancestor throughout a descendant’s execution can protect accesses in the descendant, although it never acquires the mutex. Their analysis operates on observed executions and derives cross-thread critical sections from must-happen-before information; our contribution is a sound static abstraction establishing this protection across all executions using creation, join, thread-id, and lock-history information.

9 Conclusion and Future Work

Sound static race detection comes with strong guarantees; reducing false positives is crucial for usability. We built on digests, a framework refining thread-modular abstract interpretation, by distinguishing program points according to thread histories. While previous work cast existing techniques as digests to justify their soundness, we present novel digests for several interesting concurrency primitives that have received little to no attention in sound static race detection. Future work may apply our techniques to other concurrency bugs, such as deadlocks and termination.

Appendix 0.B Proofs for Propositions 1 and 2

Recall Proposition 1 from Section 2.1:

Proposition 5

Two accesses to a global variable gg are racy in the intuitive sense if and only if at least one is a write and traces t0t_{0} and t1t_{1} ending in the respective CFG predecessors exist, s.t. they are bidirectionally trace compatible.

Proof

More formally, in line with [25], define two accesses to be racy in the intuitive sense if they access the same memory, at least one is a write, and there exists a local trace in which they are unordered after disregarding the order induced by the accesses themselves. The proof is then a simplification of the proof of [25, Theorem 1], which uses atomicity mutexes to order accesses to globals. The existence of observing actions of arity n does not complicate the proof here, as it does not consider the reason some actions are ordered w.r.t. each other. ∎

Recall Proposition 2 from Section 2.2:

Proposition 6

Refining a sound abstract interpretation of a concurrent program with an admissible digest yields a sound abstract interpretation.

Proof

First, a version of the concrete semantics where the unknowns are split according to the digests is constructed. This refined concrete semantics is shown equivalent to the original concrete semantics, which is shown by giving a bijection between least solutions of either of the constraint systems. The property is then established by fixpoint induction performing a case distinction based on the considered constraint. The proof is a (slight) generalization of the proof of Theorem 4 of Section 2.3 of the PhD thesis of Schwarz [28], to account for the higher arity of observing actions but no additional complications arise here. Then, from the soundness of the base analysis, the soundness of the refined analysis follows by checking that by concretizing a solution of the abstract refined analysis one obtains a solution of the refined concrete constraint system. This is done by verifying this property for each constraint.∎

Technically, the admissibility of the lockset digest would also need to be re-established for the additional considered actions, but as they return the digest unmodified, and pthread_once and barriers do not affect sets of held locks, this is straightforward.

The digest given in Section 3 is admissible, and its predicate ||?||^{?} is sound.

Beyond supporting pthread_once for checking for data races, one can also increase the precision of an analysis by only reading those values that globals may have after the code inside pthread_once has been executed.

A digest to help analyze this feature (Figure 10) may then track three pieces of information in a tuple (A,C,O)(A,C,O):

  • •

    Some set AA of active control variables as in Section 3.

  • •

    Some set CC of completed control variables, i.e., control variables for which the associated fragment has surely been run. Unlike in Section 3, this is not only the case if endO​(o)\textsf{endO}(o) was called by the ego thread or one of its parents, but also when the ego thread incorporates an observable action where the control variable is completed.

  • •

    Additionally, a map OO tracking for each mutex aa, for which of the control variables oo the mutex aa was unlocked while oo was active.

The interesting case is the right-hand side for acquiring a mutex aa: In case the ego thread has observed that the mutex aa was unlocked while some control variable oo was active, but the trace ending in the unlock of aa has neither observed this nor is the control variable currently active, there must have been a later unlock of aa, where the control variable was active. Thus, no two traces with such digests can be compatible.

Example 7

Consider again the program in Figure 5, and an analysis associating values of globals with mutexes that are always held when the global is accessed, refined with the digests from Figure 10. At the later lock​(md​e​v)\textsf{lock}(m_{dev}) in both of the threads, the only reaching digests of the ego threads are (∅,{o},{md​e​v↦{o}})(\emptyset,\{o\},\{m_{dev}\mapsto\{o\}\}). Thus, only those unknowns associated with observable actions with a digest (A1,C1,O1)(A_{1},C_{1},O_{1}) where oo is either in A1A_{1} or C1C_{1} can be incorporated here. For all these unknowns, the value of gg is known to not be null. Thus, the assertions can be shown in both threads. \hfill\squareforqed

Appendix 0.D Details on Barriers

We first remark on the difference between barriers and signals.

Remark 2

While the signalling mechanism of Pthreads at first glance seems similar to barriers of capacity one, the information that a call to signal_wait(s) has returned cannot help exclude data races. Pthreads allows for spurious wakeups, so such a call may return even though ss has not been signalled.

We next turn to the soundness of using this digest for excluding races. Recall that the barrier digest is built on a digest 𝒜1{\mathcal{A}}_{1}. We assume that 𝒜1{\mathcal{A}}_{1} is admissible and that its predicate ||?𝒜1||^{?}_{{\mathcal{A}}_{1}} is sound. Recall that in Section 2.2 we have established that ||?𝒜1||^{?}_{{\mathcal{A}}_{1}} can be used to check whether arbitrary actions may-happen-in-parallel. We further assume that the base abstraction is insensitive to the newly introduced barrier record and check actions. That is, extending a trace by either action does not change its 𝒜1{\mathcal{A}}_{1} abstraction, and the corresponding base right-hand sides are identity functions. As required for the generic thread IDs introduced in Section 2, πtid\pi_{\textsf{tid}} is constant along each concrete thread and unique​(q)\textsf{unique}(q) implies that at most one concrete thread in an execution has projected ID qq.

Recall the following proposition from Section 4:

Appendix 0.F Digests for Creation Locksets

We propose the digest in Figure 12 to analyze the conditions given at the end of Section 6. Such a digest is a triple ((A,S,J),C,O)((A,S,J),C,O):

  • •

    A triple (A,S,J)(A,S,J) representing the thread id and lockset digest introduced in Section 2.2, and the join digest by Schwarz and Erhard [24].

  • •

    A map CC mapping each thread id ii to a set of mutexes, where mm is included if conditions 2 and 3 are satisfied.

  • •

    A map OO mapping each thread id ii to a pair. In the digest of the ego thread, O​iO\,i stores the CC component and the set of may-created thread ids of the most recently observed sub-trace belonging to a thread represented by ii. Such an observation occurs when the ego thread locks a mutex after that thread unlocks it. We use OO to compare the lockset at a program point with inter-threaded mutex protections of other threads.

To determine if two program points with the digests explained above may race, we can evaluate the following predicate:

((A0,S0,J0),C0,O0)||?((A1,S1,J1),C1,O1)=let​i0=πtid​A0​inlet​i1=πtid​A1​in{falseif(∃iO∈TID:iO≠i1∧let(CO,IO′)=O1iOinOPENCO​i0∩S1≠∅∧({i0}∪must_anc​i0)∩IO′≠∅)∨(∃iO∈TID:iO≠i0∧let(CO,IO′)=O0iOinOPENCO​i1∩S0≠∅∧({i1}∪must_anc​i1)∩IO′≠∅)⊤otherwise\begin{array}[]{l}((A_{0},S_{0},J_{0}),C_{0},O_{0})\,||^{?}\,((A_{1},S_{1},J_{1}),C_{1},O_{1})=\\ \qquad\textbf{let}\,i_{0}=\pi_{\textsf{tid}}\,A_{0}\,\textbf{in}\\ \qquad\textbf{let}\,i_{1}=\pi_{\textsf{tid}}\,A_{1}\,\textbf{in}\\ \qquad\begin{cases}\textsf{false}&\mathrm{if\ }\begin{array}[]{l}(\exists i_{O}\in\textsf{TID}:i_{O}\neq i_{1}\land\textbf{let}\,(C_{O},I_{O}^{\prime})=O_{1}\,i_{O}\,\textbf{in}\\ \quad C_{O}\,i_{0}\cap S_{1}\neq\emptyset\;\land(\{i_{0}\}\cup\textsf{must\_anc}\,i_{0})\cap I^{\prime}_{O}\neq\emptyset)\;\lor\\ \color[rgb]{0.25,0.25,0.25}(\exists i_{O}\in\textsf{TID}:i_{O}\neq i_{0}\land\textbf{let}\,(C_{O},I_{O}^{\prime})=O_{0}\,i_{O}\,\textbf{in}\\ \color[rgb]{0.25,0.25,0.25}\quad C_{O}\,i_{1}\cap S_{0}\neq\emptyset\;\land(\{i_{1}\}\cup\textsf{must\_anc}\,i_{1})\cap I^{\prime}_{O}\neq\emptyset)\end{array}\\ \top&\mathrm{otherwise}\end{cases}\end{array}

Consider the first disjunct for the false case. It checks whether it can be shown that the access of thread i1i_{1} must happen after the access of thread i0i_{0}. Concretely, O1​iO=(CO,IO′)O_{1}\,i_{O}=(C_{O},I^{\prime}_{O}) means that i1i_{1} observed, through a lock it or one of its ancestors acquired, an action of a thread with thread id iOi_{O}. The condition ({i0}∪must_anc​i0)∩IO′≠∅({\{i_{0}\}\cup\textsf{must\_anc}\,i_{0}})\cap I^{\prime}_{O}\neq\emptyset establishes that this observation occurred after iOi_{O} had created either i0i_{0} or one of its mandatory ancestors. If CO​i0∩S1≠∅C_{O}\,i_{0}\cap S_{1}\neq\emptyset there is some mutex, say mm, that is held at the access by i1i_{1} and that was held throughout the execution of i0i_{0}. Thus, we obtain that i0i_{0} or one of its mandatory ancestors must have been created before the access in i1i_{1} occurred and mm was held throughout i0i_{0}’s execution. As i0≠i1i_{0}\neq i_{1}, for i1i_{1} to succeed in acquiring mm, it must have been released, and thus i0i_{0} must have completed its execution before i1i_{1}’s access. The second, gray disjunct checks the symmetric situation.

Some ​(B′,∅,{i↦(∅,∅)∣i∈TID})≠None.\textbf{Some }(B^{\prime},\emptyset,\{i\mapsto(\emptyset,\emptyset)\mid i\in\textsf{TID}\})\neq\textbf{None}.

We now turn to the proof of soundness of ||?||^{?}: W.l.o.g., assume the first disjunct of the false case holds. Consider t0∈γ𝒜​((A0,S0,J0),C0,O0)t_{0}\in\gamma_{\mathcal{A}}((A_{0},S_{0},J_{0}),C_{0},O_{0}) and t1∈γ𝒜​((A1,S1,J1),C1,O1)t_{1}\in\gamma_{\mathcal{A}}((A_{1},S_{1},J_{1}),C_{1},O_{1}).

Consider some thread with id iOi_{O}, from which the thread at the end of t1t_{1} has observed (CO,IO′):=O1​iO(C_{O},I^{\prime}_{O}):=O_{1}\,i_{O}. Since ({i0}∪must_anc​i0)∩IO′≠∅(\{i_{0}\}\cup\textsf{must\_anc}\,i_{0})\cap I^{\prime}_{O}\neq\emptyset, threads associated with i0i_{0} have already been transitively created. Choose s∈CO​i0∩S1s\in C_{O}\,i_{0}\cap S_{1}. By the meaning of CO​i0C_{O}\,i_{0}, thread iOi_{O} holds ss throughout the execution of every relevant thread represented by i0i_{0}. At the same time, s∈S1s\in S_{1} means that the ego thread represented by i1i_{1} holds ss at the access in t1t_{1}. Since iO≠i1i_{O}\neq i_{1}, these are different threads. Mutual exclusion orders the corresponding critical sections by →s\to_{s}, so the accesses cannot be bidirectionally trace-compatible.∎

Appendix 0.G Experimental Setup

0.G.1 Benchmark Subjects

Our benchmark sets follow the conventions of the SV-Comp software-verification competition. Each benchmark instance comprises source code together with at least one property to verify:

  • •

    no-data-race , which evaluates to true if no data race occurs in any execution of the program;

  • •

    unreach-call , which evaluates to true if the special function reach_error() is unreachable in every execution of the program; and

  • •

    other properties, which are not relevant to the benchmarks considered here.

The possible verdicts are true, false, unknown, and error. An analyzer that cannot decide a property conclusively usually returns unknown. Because SV-Comp provides no direct way to specify invariants, we encode them using program guards and the unreach-call property. Although these benchmarks are formally unreach-call tests, they let us check whether an analyzer handles synchronization features correctly.

We use a consistent naming scheme for the benchmark programs. Each filename contains four components separated by underscores. They identify, in order, the challenge (“b” for “barrier,” “cl” for “creation lockset,” “dl” for “descendant lockset,” and “o” for “once”), the property (“n” for no-data-race and “u” for unreach-call ), the expected verdict (“true” or “false”), and a number that uniquely identifies the benchmark.

0.G.2 Soundness and Precision

For both no-data-race and unreach-call , we classify verdicts as follows:

analysis verdict
TRUE FALSE
ground truth TRUE ✓{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0.5}\checkmark} false positive
FALSE false negative ✓{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0.5}\checkmark}

Under this formulation, a false positive is a FALSE verdict when TRUE is expected and indicates imprecision. A false negative is a TRUE verdict when FALSE is expected and indicates unsoundness. Because abstract interpretation overapproximates program behavior, an abstract interpreter generally cannot substantiate a FALSE verdict when FALSE is expected and therefore usually returns UNKNOWN.

0.G.3 Comparative Benchmark Baseline

We selected the baseline tools from SV-Comp participants that performed well in concurrent-program verification categories. For each tool, we used the parameters specified by its configuration for the relevant categories. RacerF is an abstract interpreter that supports only the no-data-race property, so we did not evaluate it on unreach-call .

Tool Version Configuration
Racerf 2.2 ./racerf-sv.py -machdep gcc_x86_64 $FILE
ESBMC (base) 7.7.0 ./esbmc --no-div-by-zero-check --force-malloc-success --state-hashing --add-symex-value-sets --no-align-check --k-step 2 --floatbv --unlimited-k-steps --no-vla-size-check $FILE --64 --no-por --context-bound 3 --witness-output witness.graphml --no-pointer-check --no-bounds-check --incremental-bmc
ESBMC (no-data-race) --data-races-check --no-assertions
ESBMC (unreach-call) --enable-unreachability-intrinsic
CPAChecker 4.2.2 ./cpachecker --svcomp26 --heap 10000M --benchmark --timelimit 900 s --stats --spec $PROPERTY --64 $FILE
U. Gemcutter 0.3.1 ./Ultimate.py --spec $PROPERTY --file $FILE --full-output --architecture 64bit
Dartagnan 4.1.0 ./Dartagnan-SVCOMP.sh $PROPERTY $FILE

0.G.4 Benchmark Execution Times

We ran the benchmarks on a machine with a 2.5 GHz Intel Core i7-11700 CPU, 64 GB of RAM, and Ubuntu 26.04. Each tool invocation was limited to 5 minutes and 20 GB of RAM.

0.G.5 Soundness

To assess soundness, we use no-data-race and unreach-call benchmarks whose expected verdict is FALSE and compare each tool’s result with the expected verdict. A TRUE verdict in these cases misses a data race and is therefore a false negative; a single such verdict demonstrates unsound behavior. A FALSE or UNKNOWN verdict is consistent with soundness, but an UNKNOWN verdict does not establish that the property is false. Dartagnan and Ultimate Gemcutter recognize occurrences of barriers and pthread_once but return ERROR and UNKNOWN, respectively. These inconclusive results provide no evidence of unsoundness or precision. RacerF does not support unreach-call and is therefore not evaluated for that property. Because Goblint is an overapproximating abstract interpreter, it returns UNKNOWN, rather than FALSE, for the false unreach-call properties. It could nevertheless return TRUE; such a result would be a false negative.

Benchmark Results

Example benchmarks indicating unsound behavior

To illustrate the unsoundness we found, we present compact benchmarks that the corresponding tools report as data-race-free even though they contain a data race.

Assertions provide another way to expose unsound behavior. In SV-Comp, assertions are typically encoded using the unreach-call property, which can also reveal false negatives, as one of the examples below shows.

  • •

    Racerf reports this program as data-race-free:

    ⬇
    1 // expected verdict: no-data-race false
    2 #include <pthread.h>
    3 #include <stdio.h>
    4 #include <assert.h>
    5
    6 int g = 0;
    7 pthread_once_t once = PTHREAD_ONCE_INIT;
    8
    9 void fun() {
    10 g++; // RACE
    11 }
    12
    13 void *f(void *p){
    14 fun();
    15 }
    16 pthread_t id1;
    17
    18 int main(void) {
    19 pthread_t id;
    20
    21 pthread_create(&id1, NULL, f, NULL);
    22 pthread_once(&once, fun);
    23
    24 return 0;
    25 }
  • •

    CPAChecker reports this file as data-race-free:

    ⬇
    1 // expected verdict: no-data-race false
    2 extern int __VERIFIER_nondet_int();
    3
    4 #include <pthread.h>
    5
    6 int global = 0;
    7 pthread_mutex_t mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
    8 pthread_t id1, id2;
    9
    10 void *t1(void *arg) {
    11 pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
    12 global++; // RACE!
    13 pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);
    14 return NULL;
    15 }
    16
    17 // t2 is not protected by mutex locked in main thread,
    18 // joining may not happen before unlock
    19 void *t2(void *arg) {
    20 global++; // RACE!
    21 return NULL;
    22 }
    23
    24 int main(void) {
    25 pthread_create(&id1, NULL, t1, NULL);
    26 pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
    27 pthread_create(&id2, NULL, t2, NULL);
    28 int maybe = __VERIFIER_nondet_int();
    29 if (maybe) {
    30 pthread_join(id2, NULL);
    31 }
    32 pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);
    33 return 0;
    34 }
  • •

    ESBMC and CPAChecker report that the error state in this file is unreachable:

    ⬇
    1 // expected verdict: unreach-call false
    2 #include <pthread.h>
    3 #include <stdio.h>
    4 #include <assert.h>
    5
    6 extern void abort(void);
    7 void reach_error() { assert(0); }
    8 // expected: unreach-call is false
    9 #define __VERIFIER_assert(cond) { if((cond)) { reach_error(); abort(); } }
    10
    11 int g = 0;
    12 pthread_once_t once = PTHREAD_ONCE_INIT;
    13
    14 void fun() {
    15 g++;
    16 }
    17
    18
    19 int main(void) {
    20 pthread_t id;
    21
    22 pthread_once(&once, fun);
    23 pthread_once(&once, fun);
    24
    25 __VERIFIER_assert(g==1); // g==1 is true here -> reach_error() is reached
    26
    27 return 0;
    28 }

0.G.6 Precision

To assess precision, we use no-data-race and unreach-call benchmarks whose expected verdict is TRUE and compare each tool’s result with the expected verdict. A FALSE verdict in these cases is a false positive. Dartagnan and Ultimate Gemcutter recognize occurrences of barriers and pthread_once but return ERROR and UNKNOWN, respectively. Neither result demonstrates that the tool can verify the property. RacerF does not support unreach-call and is therefore not evaluated for that property.

Benchmark Results

Example benchmarks indicating imprecise behavior

To demonstrate the kinds of imprecise behavior we found, we present compact benchmarks that some analyzers report as containing a data race but that are actually data-race-free. The following is a representative barrier example:

⬇
1 // expected verdict: no-data-race true
2 #include<pthread.h>
3 #include<stdio.h>
4 #include<unistd.h>
5
6 extern int __VERIFIER_nondet_int();
7
8 int g;
9
10 pthread_barrier_t barrier;
11
12 void* f1(void* ptr) {
13 g = 2; // NORACE
14 pthread_barrier_wait(&barrier);
15
16 return NULL;
17 }
18
19 int main(int argc, char const *argv[])
20 {
21 int top = __VERIFIER_nondet_int();
22 int i = 0;
23
24 pthread_barrier_init(&barrier, NULL, 2);
25
26 pthread_t t1;
27 pthread_create(&t1,NULL,f1,NULL);
28
29 pthread_barrier_wait(&barrier);
30 g = 3; //NORACE
31
32 return 0;
33 }
